summary: MPLS networks stack labels on packets, but not every router in the middle of a network speaks MPLS. This standards-track memo defines two ways to wrap MPLS packets inside ordinary IP or inside GRE tunnels, so MPLS-based applications can cross networks whose core does not support MPLS.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4023 defines two formats for carrying an MPLS packet through an IP network: MPLS-in-IP and MPLS-in-GRE. The far endpoint removes the outer headers and processes the packet as MPLS.

questions: how to carry mpls over ip
what ip protocol number is mpls in ip
how to secure an mpls tunnel with ipsec
subtitle: Two ways to carry MPLS packets through an IP network that does not support MPLS.

tldr.problem: MPLS label-switched paths may cross an IP network whose routers do not support MPLS.
tldr.mechanism: An MPLS packet can be carried directly inside IP using protocol number 137, or inside GRE carried over IP. The receiving tunnel endpoint removes the outer headers.
tldr.outcome: The encapsulations let MPLS traffic cross an IP core without MPLS support. The tunnels do not provide authentication, integrity, or privacy by themselves; RFC 5332 updates this RFC.

today: RFC 4023 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2005. The unit metadata says it was updated by RFC 5332.

sections.title: Why Carry MPLS Through IP
sections.content:
An MPLS label stack can contain more than one label. The top label carries a packet from one label switching router to the next, where the next router processes the label below it.

RFC 4023 allows an IP or GRE header to replace the top label as the outer delivery mechanism. The two tunnel endpoints must know the far endpoint's IP address and support for the selected encapsulation; how they learn this is outside the RFC's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS packets can cross a network that does not process MPLS if the endpoints wrap them in an IP-based tunnel. The tunnel endpoints must be configured or discovered by another method.

sections.title: MPLS-in-IP Format
sections.content:
An MPLS-in-IP packet contains an IPv4 or IPv6 header, an MPLS label stack, and one MPLS message body. The outer source and destination addresses identify the encapsulating and decapsulating routers.

The IP protocol or IPv6 next-header value is 137 for MPLS unicast. This specification does not support MPLS multicast in the direct MPLS-in-IP format. The receiving endpoint removes the IP header and processes the remaining packet using its top MPLS label.
sections.plainLanguage: The outer IP header identifies the two tunnel endpoints and marks the payload as MPLS. The receiving endpoint removes that header and continues MPLS processing.

sections.title: MPLS-in-GRE Format
sections.content:
MPLS-in-GRE places an MPLS packet after an IP header and a GRE header. The GRE protocol type must identify MPLS unicast with Ethertype 0x8847 or MPLS multicast with 0x8848.

GRE checksum, key, and sequence fields are optional and not required by this use. A receiver must handle packets without them, and a sender must omit them by default and include them only when it knows the receiver supports them.
sections.plainLanguage: The GRE format adds a GRE header between the IP header and the MPLS packet. Implementations must work without GRE's optional checksum, key, and sequence fields.

sections.title: Fragmentation, TTL and Traffic Treatment
sections.content:
Fragmentation is configurable at the tunnel head, but the default must be not to fragment. With IPv4, the head sets the Don't Fragment bit. It should use Path MTU Discovery and maintain a Tunnel MTU; an MPLS packet larger than that MTU is discarded.

The tunnel head may copy the MPLS TTL into the outer IP TTL or Hop Limit. The tail may copy the value back only if it does not increase the MPLS TTL. The outer Differentiated Services field may also reflect the MPLS packet's behavior aggregate.
sections.plainLanguage: The tunnel head tracks the size packets can use and discards packets that exceed the tunnel limit. Optional TTL and service-class handling carries selected information through the tunnel.

sections.title: Choosing an Encapsulation
sections.content:
MPLS-in-IP is the more efficient option and is generally preferable when other factors are equal. MPLS-in-GRE can be useful when two routers already communicate through a GRE tunnel or when hardware handles GRE more efficiently.

For IPv6 outer headers, the RFC says the general procedures in RFC 2473 apply. The selected method must be supported by both tunnel endpoints.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS-in-IP uses the more efficient format when there is no other constraint. MPLS-in-GRE is useful when the routers already use GRE or their implementation requires it.

sections.title: Tunnel Security
sections.content:
Neither encapsulation authenticates the sender, checks packet integrity, or hides packet contents. The significance of these risks depends on the applications using the tunnel. IPsec support is optional in the specification.

If IPsec is used, the tunnel endpoints form a Security Association and must provide authentication and integrity. Without IPsec, another method must ensure that the tail accepts only packets sent by the head; address filtering may help within one administrative domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The outer headers alone do not prove who sent a packet or whether it changed in transit. Operators who need those protections must add IPsec or another suitable mechanism.

layers.label: IP header
layers.detail: IPv4 or IPv6; protocol or next header 137
